readme.overviewHtml:
Carbon ownership, not carbon awareness.

A full-stack carbon-footprint prototype with a deterministic accounting engine, a FastAPI backend and a Next.js frontend. The repository includes security and accessibility tests; this is a student project, not a security-audited production service.


The dashboard screen. More screens in the product walkthrough.

sections.title: Project summary
sections.html:
Project summary

What it is: EarthShare is a carbon-footprint prototype. Users record everyday activities, receive deterministic emission estimates, view insights, and track progress by completing suggested climate actions.

Why it's different: Most carbon apps focus on awareness (charts, streaks, badges). EarthShare focuses on ownership (account, measure, neutralize). The behavioral model is the product.

Engineering: The backend includes JWT authentication, rate limiting, configurable CORS middleware, security headers, and request-schema validation. Carbon calculations are deterministic and do not use an LLM. SQLite is the local default; PostgreSQL migration and production deployment have not been verified.

sections.title: Local setup
sections.html:
Local setup

Prerequisites

  • Python 3.11 or another version supported by the installed backend dependencies.
  • Node.js and npm.
  • No Gemini API key is required for local use; without one, insights use the rule-based fallback.

Backend

From the repository root:

git clone https://github.com/Soham-o/EarthShare.git
cd EarthShare
python -m venv backend/.venv
# Activate the environment:
# macOS/Linux: source backend/.venv/bin/activate
# Windows PowerShell: .\backend\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install -r backend/requirements.txt

Copy backend/.env.example to backend/.env, then start the API:

# macOS/Linux
cp backend/.env.example backend/.env
# Windows PowerShell: Copy-Item backend/.env.example backend/.env

cd backend
uvicorn app.main:app --reload

The API defaults to local SQLite and is available at http://localhost:8000.

Frontend

In a second terminal from the repository root:

cd frontend
npm ci

Copy frontend/.env.example to .env.local in the frontend/ directory, then run:

# macOS/Linux
cp .env.example .env.local
# Windows PowerShell: Copy-Item .env.example .env.local

npm run dev

Open http://localhost:3000. The frontend's default API URL is http://localhost:8000. Never use the example JWT secret in a production deployment; configure a unique secret and explicit trusted CORS origins.

Tests

# Backend (from repository root, with the Python environment active)
cd backend
python -m pytest -q

# Frontend (in a second terminal, from repository root)
cd frontend
npm ci
npm test
npm run build

GitHub Actions runs backend tests, frontend tests and a frontend build for pull requests to main and pushes to main or fix/**.

sections.title: 1. Problem Statement Alignment
sections.html:
1. Problem Statement Alignment

Why the challenge exists

Individual emissions are a meaningful slice of the climate problem, but they are largely invisible to the people producing them. People want to act, but they have no reliable, low-friction way to (a) measure their impact, (b) understand what's driving it, and (c) actually neutralize it. The result is a gap between intent and action.

Why existing carbon footprint apps fail

  • Awareness without accountability. Most apps surface a number and a streak, then leave the user to feel bad. There's no mechanism to close the loop.
  • Opaque calculations. Estimates often come from black-box models or third-party APIs that can drift, fail, or change pricing — making results non-reproducible and hard to trust.
  • Heavy onboarding. Long questionnaires kill retention before the first insight.
  • Offsets are an afterthought. Where offsets exist, they are usually disconnected from the user's actual measured footprint.

Why ownership is a better behavioral model than awareness

Awareness asks: "Do you know your number?" Ownership asks: "What are you going to do about your number?"

EarthShare is designed around a single behavioral loop:

Log → Measure → Understand → Reduce or Offset → Repeat.

Every screen, every endpoint, and every data model exists to shorten the distance between a logged activity and a neutralized footprint. Ownership is the product.

sections.title: 2. Technical Excellence
sections.html:
2. Technical Excellence

Clean Architecture

The backend is organized into clearly separated layers — routes → services → repositories → models — so that business rules don't depend on framework details and the framework doesn't leak into business rules. This means:

  • Routes are thin: they parse, validate, and delegate.
  • Services own business logic and orchestrate repositories.
  • Repositories own persistence. Nothing else touches the ORM.
  • Models are plain data definitions.

Service Layer Pattern

All non-trivial logic — carbon calculation orchestration, user lifecycle, offset purchase flows, insight aggregation — lives in services. This keeps routes testable in isolation and lets us swap delivery mechanisms (HTTP today, a job runner tomorrow) without rewriting business logic.

Repository Pattern

Every database read/write goes through a repository. Benefits:

  • The database URL is centralized in configuration and SQLAlchemy sessions are injected; changing the database still requires a tested migration and deployment path.
  • Tests can substitute in-memory or fake repositories trivially.
  • Query logic is centralized and reviewable.

Dependency Separation

  • The carbon engine depends on nothing but Python stdlib and a static emission-factor table.
  • Services depend on repository interfaces, not concrete DB classes.
  • Routes depend on services, not on the ORM.
  • The frontend depends on a single typed API client, not on scattered fetch calls.

This is what makes the codebase easy to read, easy to test, and easy to extend.

API Design

  • Versioned API routes cover authentication, onboarding, dashboard data, insights, actions, progress and daily check-ins under /api/v1.
  • Consistent JSON envelopes for success and error responses.
  • Structured HTTP responses use appropriate status codes for validation, authentication, missing resources, conflicts, rate limits and server errors.
  • Stateless authentication via JWT bearer tokens.

Deterministic Carbon Engine

The core calculator is pure, deterministic, and offline. Given the same input, it always returns the same number. There is no LLM, no external API, and no randomness in the calculation path. This matters because:

  • Results are reproducible — a judge can compute them by hand.
  • Results are auditable — every factor is traceable to a source row.
  • Results are fast — calculations are O(1) lookups + arithmetic.
  • Results are offline-safe — no third-party outage can break the core product.

LLMs, if used at all, are confined to explanations and suggestions on top of the deterministic number — never inside it.

sections.title: 3. Security
sections.html:
3. Security

Security is implemented as defaults, not features.

  • JWT authentication. Stateless bearer tokens with signed payloads, expiry, and explicit verification on every protected route.
  • Password hashing. Passwords are stored using a modern adaptive hash (bcrypt-family) with per-user salts. Plaintext is never logged or returned.
  • Rate limiting. Sensitive endpoints (login, register, password actions) are rate-limited to blunt brute-force and credential-stuffing attempts.
  • CORS configuration. Allowed origins are loaded from the CORS_ORIGINS environment setting. Configure explicit trusted origins in deployments; the current configuration code does not reject a wildcard automatically.
  • Security headers. API responses include Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy. HSTS is enabled for production deployments.
  • Input validation. Typed request schemas validate inputs before route handlers call services. Schema-validation errors are typically returned as structured HTTP 422 responses; they should not expose stack traces.
  • Error handling. Unexpected exceptions return a generic JSON error, while the server logs the exception with the request method and path. A correlation ID is not currently implemented.

Secrets (JWT signing key, DB URL, allowed origins) are loaded from environment variables only — never committed.

sections.title: 4. Testing
sections.html:
4. Testing

Backend test suite

  • Unit tests for the carbon engine (pure functions → exhaustive table-driven cases).
  • Unit tests for services with repositories stubbed.
  • Integration tests for routes spinning up the app against an ephemeral SQLite DB.
  • Auth tests covering registration, login, token expiry, and protected-route rejection.

Frontend test suite

  • Component tests cover the daily check-in card, emissions equity ring, form field, option grid and accessibility assertions.
  • The current suite is not a complete end-to-end test of all user journeys; manual screen-reader and keyboard-only review has not been verified.

Continuous integration

  • GitHub Actions runs the backend test suite, frontend tests and a frontend production build on pull requests and pushes to main and fix/** branches.
  • Latest verified run: 85 backend tests passed, 1 skipped; 21 frontend tests passed; frontend build succeeded. See the CI run.

Coverage notes

  • Tests exercise the carbon engine, API routes, authentication, daily check-ins, security headers and selected frontend components.
  • The CI suite is a useful regression baseline, not a security certification or proof that every feature is covered.

sections.title: 5. Accessibility
sections.html:
5. Accessibility

EarthShare targets a WCAG 2.1 AA mindset throughout the UI.

  • Keyboard navigation. Every interactive element is reachable and operable via keyboard. Logical tab order, visible focus rings, and no keyboard traps.
  • Screen reader support. Semantic HTML first (<button>, <nav>, <main>, <form>, <label>). Live regions announce async results (e.g. "Activity logged, 2.3 kg CO₂e added").
  • ARIA labels. Used to supplement semantics where native HTML can't express intent (icon-only buttons, dynamic counts, modal dialogs).
  • WCAG-conscious design. Color is never the only signal; text contrast targets AA ratios; form errors are associated with their inputs via aria-describedby.
  • Responsive layouts. Mobile-first CSS, fluid typography, and breakpoints that keep tap targets ≥ 44px. The dashboard, insights, and marketplace are all usable on a phone in portrait.

sections.title: 6. Efficiency
sections.html:
6. Efficiency

Why deterministic calculations are computationally efficient

The carbon engine is a pure function over a static emission-factor table. Each calculation is effectively:

emissions = activity_quantity × factor[activity_type][region]

For one activity, the calculation uses a constant-time factor-table lookup and arithmetic; no performance benchmark is published in this repository.

Why local calculations reduce API dependency

The carbon calculation engine runs locally within the backend and uses an in-repository factor table:

  • The calculation itself does not require a third-party API call.
  • Its calculation path has no per-request model/API fee.
  • The factor table can be inspected and versioned with the source.
  • Optional insight generation and other app features may still use external services when configured.

Why SQLite was chosen for hackathon deployment simplicity

  • Zero-ops: the database is a file. No provisioning, no separate service, no credentials to rotate during a demo.
  • Instant local dev: clone, install, run.
  • Trivial CI: tests run against an ephemeral in-memory DB.
  • Automated backend tests use an in-memory SQLite database; live hosting parity has not been verified.

Database configuration and migration status

The database URL is centralized in backend/app/core/config.py, and the app uses SQLAlchemy sessions and repository classes. SQLite is the verified local/test default. PostgreSQL migration, migrations against a PostgreSQL instance, and production deployment have not been verified, so a connection-string change alone should not be presented as a proven migration path.

sections.title: 7. Why We Chose This Architecture
sections.html:
7. Why We Chose This Architecture

Goal: Maximize judge-perceivable quality and maximize how far the codebase can travel after the hackathon.

Decision Why What it buys us
Clean Architecture (routes → services → repos → models) Keeps business rules independent of framework and DB Easy to test, easy to refactor, easy to read
Service layer One place for business logic; routes stay thin Reusable logic across HTTP, jobs, and tests
Repository pattern One place for persistence Centralizes database access; alternate-database migration still needs validation
Deterministic carbon engine Reproducibility and auditability beat cleverness here Repeatable calculations from a versioned factor table
JWT authentication Uses signed bearer tokens Avoids a server-side session table for token state; production scale is not evaluated
SQLite for v1 Zero-ops for the demo Reliable hackathon-day deploy
Configurable database URL Keeps the connection setting in one place PostgreSQL compatibility remains unverified
Typed API client on the frontend Single source of truth for request/response shapes Fewer integration bugs, better DX
Accessibility tests Catch selected accessibility regressions early Automated accessibility assertions exist; full WCAG conformance is not claimed
LLMs out of the calculation path Determinism > novelty for a measurement product Numbers a judge can verify by hand

The prototype separates routes, services, repositories, models and schemas, but production readiness, hosted deployment and database migration still need independent validation.

sections.title: 11. What Makes EarthShare Different
sections.html:
11. What Makes EarthShare Different

  • Measure clearly. The app estimates emissions from user-entered activity and an in-repository factor table.
  • Deterministic calculation. The carbon engine does not call an LLM to calculate emissions.
  • Action-oriented workflow. Suggested actions can be marked complete and reflected in progress.
  • Security and accessibility checks. The repository has automated tests for selected behaviors; it has not undergone a security audit or full accessibility conformance review.
  • Prototype status. Live deployment, production scaling and PostgreSQL migration remain unverified.

sections.title: 12. Evidence of Engineering Quality
sections.html:
12. Evidence of Engineering Quality

Engineering signals a reviewer can verify in minutes

  • Services contain no SQL. Open any service file and confirm.
  • The deterministic carbon calculation is implemented in backend/app/services/carbon_engine.py.
  • Authentication dependencies and security configuration live under backend/app/core/.
  • The frontend API wrapper is frontend/src/lib/api.ts.

readme.overviewHtml:
A Streamlit decision-support prototype for urban air-quality interventions

AirTwin X takes a city's current air-quality reading and walks it through a pipeline: estimate which sources are driving the pollution, rank a fixed set of municipal interventions, simulate what combining them would do, and translate the predicted improvement into health and economic estimates. A rule-based "Mayor Copilot" answers questions using only the outputs of those earlier steps.

Screenshots / demo GIF: not yet captured. Run it locally with the Quick Start to see the interface.

sections.title: The idea
sections.html:
The idea

Most city AQI dashboards report a number and a generic warning, then stop. They describe the problem but don't help anyone decide what to do about it. Simply wrapping a large language model around a sensor feed doesn't fix that either: a generative model can produce confident but untraceable impact estimates, and will often add intervention effects together as if they were independent.

AirTwin X treats the problem as a decision pipeline instead:

  • When two interventions target the same pollution source, their effects compound rather than add: the remaining share of a source is Π (1 − effectiveness_i), and the combined reduction is capped.
  • Every number the Copilot reports comes from an upstream module's output. It does not generate free-form text from a language model.

sections.title: What it does
sections.html:
What it does

Module File What is implemented
Source attribution attribution_engine.py Splits current AQI into Traffic, Construction, Industrial, Biomass Burning and Weather Amplification percentages using OpenStreetMap road data, weather telemetry and fire-hotspot data, with a confidence score and the list of data sources actually used.
Intervention ranking intervention_agent.py Scores 8 predefined interventions with a weighted multi-criteria formula (AQI impact 0.40, cost 0.20, feasibility 0.20, confidence 0.10, speed 0.10), a simplified TOPSIS-style weighting.
Scenario simulation ("digital twin") intervention_agent.py simulate_scenario() / compare_scenarios() apply the overlap-compounding rule above to one or more selected interventions.
Health & economic impact health_economic_engine.py Converts a predicted PM2.5 reduction into estimated admissions avoided, DALYs and cost savings. Deterministic, with its assumptions listed in the output.
Mayor Copilot mayor_copilot.py Deterministic keyword-based intent matching over the outputs above. No LLM.
Dashboard app.py Streamlit UI with Folium maps and Plotly charts, an hourly AQI projection from an XGBoost model trained on synthetic data (see limitations), and route planning that uses a PPO agent if a trained model is present, falling back to Dijkstra otherwise.

System architecture

flowchart TD
    subgraph Data["Data sources"]
        W[WAQI sensors]
        M[Open-Meteo weather]

Each stage is a plain Python module with its own tests, and every number the Copilot reports comes from an earlier stage rather than a language model. Dotted lines are the fallbacks used when a token or key is not configured.

See Architecture.md for each module's inputs, outputs and design decisions.

sections.title: Quick Start
sections.html:
Quick Start

git clone https://github.com/Soham-o/AirTwin-X.git
cd AirTwin-X
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate        # Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
streamlit run app.py

Then open http://localhost:8501. New Delhi is selected by default.

requirements.txt includes torch and stable-baselines3, so the first install is large. A .devcontainer/ configuration is also included.

sections.title: Data sources and configuration
sections.html:
Data sources and configuration

Source Used for Configuration
WAQI Live sensor readings Optional WAQI_TOKEN in .streamlit/secrets.toml or as an environment variable. Without it, the app shows a warning and uses simulated sensor data.
Open-Meteo Wind and temperature No key needed.
OpenStreetMap (via osmnx) Road network for traffic attribution No key needed. new_delhi_5km.graphml is included as a local graph.
NASA FIRMS Fire hotspots for biomass attribution Optional NASA_FIRMS_MAP_KEY environment variable. Without a key, the app skips the request and uses the Open-Meteo-based heuristic.

Never commit .streamlit/secrets.toml or real API tokens.

sections.title: Testing
sections.html:
Testing

pip install pytest numpy requests
python -m pytest test_airtwin.py -q

test_airtwin.py contains 29 tests covering determinism, intervention ranking weights, overlap-compounding bounds, CPCB AQI→PM2.5 breakpoints, health-impact monotonicity, Copilot intent routing, and missing/configured NASA FIRMS key behavior. They need only numpy, requests and pytest, not the full Streamlit stack. GitHub Actions runs these regression tests on pull requests and pushes to main or fix/** branches.

sections.title: Project status
sections.html:
Project status

Prototype. The pipeline modules and their tests run locally. Outputs are model-based estimates for exploring policy options, not validated forecasts, and should not be used for real public-health or budget decisions.

sections.title: Known limitations
sections.html:
Known limitations

  • NASA FIRMS data is optional. Set NASA_FIRMS_MAP_KEY in the environment to enable fire-hotspot requests. Without it, the app skips the request and uses the documented Open-Meteo-based heuristic. Do not commit the key.
  • No trained RL model is committed. app.py looks for a clean_air_agent PPO model; without it, routing uses Dijkstra. Train one with train_agent.py.
  • The XGBoost AQI projection is trained on synthetic data generated in app.py (daily cycles plus noise around the current reading), not on historical sensor data.
  • Attribution weights and intervention effectiveness values are fixed assumptions in the source code, not values fitted to measured data.
  • Fallbacks are silent in places. If WAQI is unavailable the dashboard switches to simulated data with a warning; check the data-source labels in the UI before trusting a number.
  • No license file has been added yet.

readme.overviewHtml:
Intelligence at your cursor.

A privacy-first, local-first Windows assistant that appears around your mouse cursor when you press a hotkey — translate, explain, summarize, rewrite, ask AI, search, or pull text off the screen, without leaving whatever you're already looking at.

The radial menu widget from ui/radial_menu.py, rendered offscreen by scripts/render_radial_preview.py. Fonts may differ slightly from Windows.

Demo GIF: not yet captured. A recording of the full flow (hotkey → menu → result panel) needs a Windows machine. The fastest way to see it is to run it: Quick Start takes about two minutes on a machine that already has Python.

sections.title: Why
sections.html:
Why

Every one of these actions already exists somewhere — a translator site, a chat app, a search bar. What doesn't exist is one of them appearing exactly where your mouse already is, the instant you ask for it, without a tab switch, a paste, or an account. Select some text — a browser, a PDF, an IDE, a chat window — press Ctrl+Alt+B, and a menu appears at your cursor. Pick an action, and the answer opens right there.

sections.title: Quick Start
sections.html:
Quick Start

python -m venv venv
venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements-core.txt
python main.py

Press Ctrl+Alt+B anywhere. That's the whole app — no account, no setup wizard, no window to find. See SETUP_GUIDE.md for a full fresh-machine walkthrough and how to add the optional engines (translation, AI, OCR) behind each action.

Also working: a customizable global hotkey (native RegisterHotKey / WM_HOTKEY, no keyboard hooks), a cursor-anchored radial menu with full mouse and keyboard navigation, multi-monitor and DPI-aware positioning, clipboard-safe selection capture, a real Settings/Privacy/Check-Components tray UI, and graceful degradation — every optional engine above is independently optional, and a fresh install with none of them present still starts and runs, disabling exactly the one action each is missing.

At startup, Cursor Bite performs zero network requests and initializes zero optional components. Nothing is imported, probed, or connected to until an action needs it.

flowchart TD
    C[Selected text or screen capture] --> G[Privacy gateway scans for emails, API keys,<br/>tokens, card numbers, private IPs, credential pairs]
    G --> Q{Does the action<br/>leave the device?}
    Q -->|"No: Translate, Explain, Summarize,<br/>Rewrite, Ask AI, OCR"| L[Processed locally,<br/>sensitive or not]
    Q -->|Yes: Search Web| E{Sensitive<br/>data found?}
    E -->|No| S[Sent to DuckDuckGo]
    E -->|Yes| B[Blocked, or ask consent<br/>with a redacted preview]
  • Local first. Translation, AI, and OCR all run on your machine. Search is the only action that sends anything off it, and the app tells you before it does.
  • Sensitive data never leaves the device unintentionally. Detected patterns never block local processing — the text is already on your machine, and blocking it there would make the app useless for the documents you most want help with. They do block, or require explicit consent for, anything that would send them externally.
  • Your clipboard is yours. Snapshotted and restored on every path, including the ones where capture failed or was cancelled.
  • No telemetry, no keylogging, no continuous screen or clipboard monitoring. Capture only happens when you explicitly invoke it.
  • No user content in the logs — action names, durations, and error types, never your text, prompts, translations, or search queries.

The detector is regex-based and documented as a safety net, not a guarantee — see SECURITY.md for its threat model and known limitations.

sections.title: Architecture
sections.html:
Architecture

sequenceDiagram
    actor U as You
    participant H as Hotkey listener<br/>(RegisterHotKey)
    participant C as Controller<br/>(UI thread)
    participant W as Worker threads<br/>(capture, pipeline)
    participant G as Privacy gateway
    U->>H: Ctrl+Alt+B
    H->>C: show radial menu at cursor now
    C-)W: capture selection in parallel
    U->>C: pick an action
    C->>W: prepare()
    W->>G: evaluate(text, requires_external)
    G-->>W: allow / needs consent / block
    W-->>C: prepared request
    opt needs consent (Search Web with sensitive text)
        C->>U: consent dialog with redacted preview
        U-->>C: approve or decline
    end
    C->>W: execute()
    W-->>C: result
    C->>U: result panel near the cursor

Ports-and-adapters layering: ui/ and app/ depend on domain/ interfaces, infrastructure/ implements them, and domain/ depends on nothing else. Providers resolve lazily and fail safe, which is what makes the startup and degradation guarantees above hold — see app/pipeline.py's _load() for the pattern.

The pipeline is split into prepare() (extract + privacy decision) and execute() (do the work) specifically so a consent dialog has a seam to sit in: it runs on the UI thread between the two phases, with the actual work on either side running on a worker thread. Decline, and nothing had run yet — nothing was sent.

├── app/              orchestration: controller, pipeline, event bus
├── domain/           interfaces + pure data, no infrastructure imports
├── infrastructure/
│   ├── ai/           Ollama
│   ├── ocr/          Tesseract
│   ├── os/           hotkey, cursor, clipboard, selection, screen capture
│   ├── privacy/      sensitive-data detector, policy engine, gateway
│   ├── search/       DuckDuckGo
│   ├── storage/      cache (in-memory); an unused-by-default SQLite option
│   └── translation/  Argos Translate
├── ui/               PyQt6: radial menu, result panel, dialogs, tray
├── config/           defaults + config.json loader
├── utils/            logging, the run_async threading helper
├── tests/            unit / integration / security
├── scripts/          dev utilities (README preview render)
└── design/           a browser-based UI/UX prototype — not the shipped app,

Technology

Python 3.11+ · PyQt6 · pywin32 · Argos Translate (offline) · Ollama (local) · Tesseract (offline) · DuckDuckGo (no API key). Every dependency is free — no paid API, no required account, no mandatory cloud service.

sections.title: Current Status
sections.html:
Current Status

Working today, exercised by the test suite and by running the app: hotkey, radial menu, tray, privacy gateway, all seven actions listed above, Settings/Privacy/Check-Components windows, clipboard-safe capture, graceful degradation of every optional engine.

Experimental: DuckDuckGo search depends on an HTML endpoint DuckDuckGo doesn't officially support for automation; it can return a bot-check page under load, which is reported plainly rather than silently retried forever. Language auto-detection for translation uses a three-tier fallback (Unicode script → statistical detection → a weak last-resort probe) that is deliberately conservative about guessing a language with no real evidence — see CHANGELOG.md for a bug this caught.

Planned, not built: Read Aloud (TTS) — the interface for it (TTSProvider in domain/interfaces.py) exists, nothing implements it yet. An installer/MSI beyond the current PyInstaller build. A packaged .exe verified end-to-end (see PACKAGING.md for exactly what has and hasn't been runtime-checked).

sections.title: Roadmap
sections.html:
Roadmap

  • Read Aloud via a local TTS engine.
  • An MSI/installer instead of a copy-the-folder EXE build.
  • Revisit the radial menu against a compact command-bar alternative with real usage data — the interaction model isn't assumed to be final.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.html:
Limitations

  • Windows only, by design.
  • Selection capture uses a simulated Ctrl+C plus a clipboard snapshot — there is no universal cross-application "get selection" API on Windows without deeper accessibility integration. This works in the overwhelming majority of apps; a handful of unusual ones (custom-rendered canvases with no text layer, some elevated/protected windows) won't produce a selection to copy. The app tells you plainly when nothing was captured rather than guessing.
  • Web search quality is bounded by an unofficial HTML endpoint — see Current Status above.
  • The sensitive-data detector is pattern-based, not exhaustive — see SECURITY.md.

sections.title: 💡 The Problem
sections.html:
💡 The Problem

New ideas are easier to remember when they are tied to something you already know well. Standard textbooks explain every topic the same way for every reader.

sections.title: 🛠️ The Solution
sections.html:
🛠️ The Solution

PersonaLearn sends each topic to Google Gemini with a prompt that asks for an explanation framed around the learner's chosen interest.

  • Don't understand Trigonometry? Read an explanation based on Cricket.
  • Confused by Blockchain? Learn it through Minecraft block analogies.

sections.title: ✨ Key Features
sections.html:
✨ Key Features

  • Preset syllabi: Topic lists for School, SSC, UPSC, and General Knowledge.
  • Interest mapping: Choose an analogy theme (Minecraft, Cricket, Marvel, Cooking, K-Pop) plus length and complexity.
  • Two views:
    • 🎓 Student view: Learn topics, mark them complete, and see a quiz score.
    • 👨‍🏫 Professor view: Add or remove syllabus topics.
  • AI quiz generator: Generates a multiple-choice question from the explanation that was just shown.
  • Scoring: Running score and quiz count for the current session.

sections.title: Why CalmReader
sections.html:
Why CalmReader

Most reading software optimizes for one metric: time on screen. The result is an environment filled with progress bars, streaks, recommendation feeds, and pop-up encouragement — tools designed to retain your attention, not support your comprehension.

The neuroscience tells a different story. Comprehension depends on working memory — a small, effortful workspace that holds ideas in active relation to each other. Every interruption taxes that workspace. Distraction isn't a minor annoyance; it's the mechanism by which understanding fails to form.

CalmReader is the antithesis of that design pattern. It is a page built like a well-made notebook: it loads your text, gets out of the way, and trusts you to read slowly. When you encounter a hard concept, it surfaces a definition — inline, quietly — without sending you down a browser tab rabbit hole. When you finish a section, it asks one good question instead of offering a five-star rating prompt.

It does not want you to keep using it. It wants you to finish reading.

sections.title: Philosophy
sections.html:
Philosophy

CalmReader is grounded in Calm Technology principles articulated by Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown: technology should require only as much attention as it deserves, communicate information at the periphery rather than the center, and amplify the best of human capability.

In practice, this means:

  • No feeds or discovery. You bring the text. CalmReader reads it with you.
  • No streaks, no badges, no gamification. Reading is intrinsically worth doing.
  • No notifications, ever. The page is silent unless you ask it something.
  • No tracking. Your reflections live locally, on your device, under your control.
  • Deep learning over content consumption. The goal is one idea truly understood, not thirty articles skimmed.

sections.title: Features
sections.html:
Features

Import Anything

Bring your own content. Paste raw text directly, upload a .txt or .md file, or pull in any article via URL using the Jina Reader proxy. No account required. No content library. Just your text.

Flow Focus

As you read, paragraphs outside your current position softly dim — reducing visual noise and keeping your working memory focused on one idea at a time. Enable it when you want it. Disable it when you don't.

Socratic Margin

CalmReader doesn't summarize — it questions. When you tap a paragraph, a context-aware prompt appears in the margin: "Does the conclusion necessarily follow?" or "What would someone who disagrees say?" These aren't generic questions. They're selected based on what the paragraph is doing — making a causal claim, citing evidence, or issuing a value judgment.

Your answer goes into the Wisdom Ledger. Not the AI's summary. Yours.

X-Ray Clarification

Forty-plus academic and conceptual terms are quietly annotated beneath the surface. Tap a term — neuroplasticity, heuristic, externality — and its definition expands inline. Reading continues. You never leave the page.

Wisdom Ledger

A running log of insights you've written during a session. Every entry is authored by you, not generated. The ledger is searchable, exportable, and stored locally.

Reflection Archive

Every insight and Pause Point response is saved across sessions in localStorage/IndexedDB. Search your own thinking across every text you've ever read in CalmReader: type a concept and find the thought you had about it three months ago.

Pause Points

Every six paragraphs, a quiet interstitial appears: "Without looking back — what do you remember?" A small text field invites active recall, which cognitive science identifies as one of the most reliable mechanisms for long-term retention. Not a quiz. Not a score. A question.

E-ink Inspired Design

Warm paper tones (#F9F6F0), generous line height, and two typefaces chosen for reading: Literata for body text and Atkinson Hyperlegible for UI — a typeface designed by the Braille Institute to maximize legibility for readers with low vision.

sections.title: Getting Started
sections.html:
Getting Started

Prerequisites

  • Node.js v18 or higher
  • pnpm (recommended) or npm

Quick Start

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/yourusername/calmreader.git
cd calmreader

# Install dependencies
pnpm install

# Start the development server
pnpm dev

Open http://localhost:5173 and paste any text to begin.

Build for Production

pnpm build
pnpm preview

The production build outputs to dist/ and is deployable to any static host (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages).

sections.title: Local Development
sections.html:
Local Development

Environment

CalmReader has no backend and requires no environment variables for local development. Everything runs in the browser.

# Development server with hot module replacement
pnpm dev

# Type checking (if using TypeScript migration branch)
pnpm typecheck

# Lint
pnpm lint

# Run all checks before committing
pnpm check

Storage

CalmReader uses two storage mechanisms:

Scope Mechanism Purpose
Session insights useState Current reading session only
Reflection archive localStorage Persists across sessions, searched globally

The storage layer is abstracted behind a simple adapter interface, designed for future migration to IndexedDB (larger archives) or native SQLite (desktop/mobile). See packages/core/src/storage/ for details.

URL Import

The URL import feature proxies requests through Jina Reader (https://r.jina.ai/{url}). No API key is required. This makes no requests unless you explicitly use the Link tab — and it is the only network call CalmReader ever makes after the initial page load.

sections.html:
Project Structure

calmreader/
├── src/
│   ├── CalmReader.jsx          # Root component — all reading UI
│   ├── main.jsx                # React entry point
│   ├── storage/
│   │   ├── adapter.ts          # StorageAdapter interface
│   │   ├── idb.ts              # IndexedDB implementation
│   │   └── index.ts            # Platform detection, exports adapter
│   ├── lib/
│   │   ├── parser.js           # parseImportedText, buildSegments
│   │   ├── prompts.js          # SOCRATIC_BANK, getPromptForParagraph
│   │   └── terms.js            # TERM_DICTIONARY (X-Ray definitions)
│   └── assets/
│       └── fonts/              # Bundled Literata + Atkinson Hyperlegible
│
├── public/
│   ├── manifest.json           # PWA manifest
│   └── sw.js                   # Service worker (offline support)
│
├── docs/
│   └── screenshots/            # README images
│
├── index.html
├── vite.config.js
├── package.json
└── README.md

Key Design Decisions

Single-file component architecture. CalmReader.jsx is intentionally large. This is not technical debt — it is a deliberate reflection of the product's philosophy. One text. One session. One file. Splitting it into twenty micro-components would add navigation overhead with no user benefit.

No state management library. CalmReader uses only useState, useEffect, useMemo, and useRef. The state surface is small enough that Redux or Zustand would be ceremony, not architecture.

No UI component library. Every visual element is hand-crafted with inline styles. This keeps the design system tight, makes the palette explicit, and means there are no Tailwind or MUI overrides to fight against.

sections.title: Roadmap
sections.html:
Roadmap

CalmReader is being developed with the principles of the deployment strategy already in mind. Each platform phase shares the same core — no parallel codebases.

Now — v1.0

  • Flow Focus (Deep Focus mode)
  • Socratic Margin with user-written insights
  • X-Ray Clarification
  • Wisdom Ledger with search
  • Reflection Archive (localStorage-backed)
  • Active recall Pause Points
  • E-ink-inspired typography system
  • PWA manifest

Next — v1.1

  • Full offline support via service worker
  • IndexedDB migration for larger archives
  • Export archive as Markdown or JSON
  • Custom term definitions (bring your own X-Ray glossary)
  • Dark mode (ink-on-black, not blue-dark)

Later — v2.0

  • Android app via Capacitor
  • iOS app via Capacitor

Someday — v3.0

sections.title: Contributing
sections.html:
Contributing

Contributions are welcome. CalmReader is a small, focused project — please keep that spirit in mind when proposing changes.

Before You Open a PR

  • Read the Philosophy section. Features that add friction, gamification, or distraction will not be merged — even if they're well-implemented.
  • Open an issue first for anything beyond a small bug fix. Discuss the shape of the change before writing code.
  • Prefer editing existing files over adding new ones. Prefer simpler over more abstract.

Development Workflow

# Fork the repository and clone your fork
git clone https://github.com/yourusername/calmreader.git

# Create a feature branch
git checkout -b feature/your-feature-name

# Make your changes, then run checks
pnpm check

# Commit with a clear message
git commit -m "feat: add custom glossary support for X-Ray terms"

# Push and open a pull request
git push origin feature/your-feature-name

What We Welcome

  • Bug fixes
  • Accessibility improvements
  • New X-Ray term definitions (edit src/lib/terms.js)
  • New Socratic prompts (edit src/lib/prompts.js)
  • Performance improvements
  • Documentation improvements
  • Platform-specific shell work (extension, desktop, mobile)

What Belongs in a Fork

  • Sync to a cloud service (unless privacy-preserving and opt-in)
  • Social features (sharing, public profiles)
  • AI-generated summaries or insights
  • Gamification of any kind

VoterOS is an interactive, AI-powered system designed to demystify the electoral process. It shifts civic engagement from reactive searching to proactive orchestration. 🛑 Why VoterOS is NOT a Chatbot

Standard AI chatbots fail in civic tech because they rely on the user to know what to ask. VoterOS flips the script:

Feature Standard Chatbot VoterOS 🚀

sections.title: ✨ Core Features

✨ Core Features

🧪 1. The Scenario Simulator ("What if...?")

The standout feature. Users can test edge cases in a safe, visual environment:

  • 📉 "What if I miss the registration deadline?" → Explains immediate disqualification.
  • ⏰ "What if I go at 10 AM?" → Triggers peak-hour congestion warnings & suggests alternatives.
  • 🪪 "What if I lost my EPIC card?" → Highlights alternative verification paths without resetting progress.

🧠 2. Hybrid AI Copilot (Gemini-Powered)

A conversational interface that feels human but acts systematically. It parses user intent, cross-references it with electoral rules, and guides the user forward.

🚇 3. Dynamic Voting Timeline

A visual flowchart (Subway Map) that maps the user's journey. It highlights the current step and visually branches when alternative paths (like Form 8 for relocation) are required.

📊 4. Voter Readiness & Confidence Engine

A real-time progress metric (0-100%). The system explicitly flags missing requirements (e.g., Address Verification Pending) and provides the immediate next action.

📑 5. Smart Form Recommender & ID Builder

Dynamically advises users on the exact documentation needed. Automatically detects if a user requires Form 6 (New Voter), Form 8 (Relocation), or Form 6A (Overseas Indian).

📈 6. Crowd Prediction Engine

A predictive bimodal curve highlighting anticipated peak wait times at the polling booth, recommending personalized "Green Zone" voting windows.

sections.title: 📍 Overview
sections.html:
📍 Overview

This project analyzes a dataset of Spotify tracks to identify distinct clusters of songs based on their audio characteristics (e.g., danceability, energy, acousticness).

By applying Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction and K-Means Clustering, we segment songs into groups. These clusters are then used to power a Content-Based Recommendation System that suggests songs mathematically similar to a user's input.

Key Features

🔍 Exploratory Analysis 🤖 Machine Learning 🎵 Recommendation
Correlation Heatmaps:
Identify relationships between audio features.		 PCA:
Reduces high-dimensional data for visualization.		 Cluster Matching:
Finds songs within the same geometric cluster.
Distribution Plots:
Analyze the spread of genres and audio attributes.		 K-Means:
Segments songs into 5 distinct genre/style clusters.		 Similarity Check:
Filters recommendations based on feature proximity.

sections.title: 🧠 Methodology
sections.html:
🧠 Methodology

The project follows a standard Data Science pipeline:

  1. Data Preprocessing: * Removal of duplicates and missing values.
    • Dropping non-numeric identifiers (track_id, track_uri, etc.).
  2. Feature Standardization: * Uses StandardScaler to normalize features (Mean=0, Std=1) so that high-magnitude features (like Loudness) don't dominate the distance calculations.
  3. Dimensionality Reduction:
    • PCA (Principal Component Analysis) is applied to compress the 9 audio features into 2 primary components for visualization purposes.
  4. Clustering:
    • K-Means Algorithm groups the data into 5 clusters (k=5).
    • $$\text{Minimize } \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{x \in S_i} || x - \mu_i ||^2$$

sections.title: 📍 Overview
sections.html:
📍 Overview

This project is a Content-Based Recommendation System built using Python and Streamlit. It solves the problem of "choice paralysis" by analyzing metadata from the TMDB 5000 Movie Dataset to suggest movies that share narrative, thematic, or production similarities with a user's selection.

Key Features

🚀 Performance 🎨 UX/UI 🔧 Engineering
Instant Results:
Generates 5 recommendations in milliseconds using pre-computed similarity matrices.		 Visual Posters:
Fetches high-res movie posters dynamically via the TMDB API.		 Vectorization:
Uses CountVectorizer to convert text data into numerical vectors.
Smart Filtering:
Filters based on a combined logic of Cast, Crew, Keywords, and Genres.		 Responsive Design:
Clean, mobile-friendly interface powered by Streamlit.		 Cosine Similarity:
Computes the geometric distance between movie vectors to find matches.

sections.title: 🧠 How It Works
sections.html:
🧠 How It Works

The engine uses Cosine Similarity to measure the distance between movies in a multi-dimensional space.

  1. Data Cleaning: We merge the Credits and Movies datasets.
  2. Feature Engineering: We create a unified tags column by concatenating:
    • Movie Overview
    • Genres
    • Keywords
    • Top 3 Cast Members
    • Director
  3. Vectorization: We remove stop words and apply stemming, then convert the text tags into 5000-dimensional vectors.
  4. Similarity Metric: We calculate the cosine of the angle between vectors. A smaller angle implies higher similarity.

$$\text{Cosine Similarity}(A, B) = \frac{A \cdot B}{|A| |B|}$$

This system uses TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) for feature extraction and Logistic Regression for classification, offering high accuracy with minimal computational cost.

sections.title: 🚀 Project Overview
sections.html:
🚀 Project Overview

Misinformation is a growing problem in the digital age. This project builds a binary classifier to distinguish between:

  • Real News: Verified articles from legitimate sources.
  • Fake News: Fabricated stories intended to deceive.

sections.title: 🛠️ Tech Stack
sections.html:
🛠️ Tech Stack

  • Python 3.x
  • Pandas & NumPy: For efficient data manipulation.
  • Scikit-Learn:
    • TfidfVectorizer: Converts text into numerical vectors based on word importance.
    • LogisticRegression: A robust linear model for binary classification.
    • Pipeline: Streamlines the training process.

sections.title: 📂 Dataset Structure
sections.html:
📂 Dataset Structure

The project expects two CSV files in the root directory: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/clmentbisaillon/fake-and-real-news-dataset

Note: The dataset is typically sourced from the ISOT Fake News Dataset or Kaggle.

sections.title: 🧠 How It Works
sections.html:
🧠 How It Works

The code follows a clean 4-step pipeline:

  1. Data Loading & Cleaning:
    • Loads the raw CSV files.
    • Assigns labels (1 for True, 0 for Fake).
    • Combines, shuffles, and removes duplicate entries to prevent data leakage.
  2. Preprocessing (TF-IDF):
    • Converts raw text into a matrix of TF-IDF features.
    • This statistically measures how important a word is to a document in the corpus.
  3. Model Training:
    • The processed vectors are fed into a Logistic Regression classifier.
  4. Evaluation:
    • Outputs the accuracy score and a detailed classification report (Precision, Recall, F1-Score).

readme.overviewHtml:
🏠 Project 1: California Housing Price Predictor (hpd.ipynb) A linear regression model designed to predict the median house value based on various geographical and demographic features. This project demonstrates how to handle mixed data types (numerical and categorical) within a single processing pipeline.

🛠️ Key Technical Features Data Handling: Implements a HousingModel class structure for modularity.

Advanced Preprocessing: Uses ColumnTransformer to apply different transformations to specific subsets of features:

Numerical Data: Median imputation for missing values followed by Standard Scaling.

Categorical Data: One-Hot Encoding (with handle_unknown='ignore') for the ocean_proximity feature.

Model: Linear Regression.

📊 Performance The model was evaluated on a 20% test split: | Metric | Value | | :--- | :--- | | RMSE | ~$70,059 | | R² Score | 0.6254 |

📧 Project 2: Spam Mail Classifier (smd.ipynb) A Natural Language Processing (NLP) classifier capable of distinguishing between "Spam" and "Ham" (legitimate) emails. This project moves beyond simple structured data into text mining and probability-based classification.

🛠️ Key Technical Features Text Cleaning: Custom Regex implementation to remove non-alphabetic characters.

NLP Pipeline:

Tokenization & Lowercasing.

Stopword Removal: Utilizing NLTK's corpus to remove noise words.

Stemming: Applied PorterStemmer to reduce words to their root form.

Vectorization: transformed text data using TfidfVectorizer (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency).

Model: Multinomial Naive Bayes (MultinomialNB), chosen for its efficiency in high-dimensional text data.

Stratification: Utilized stratified splitting to maintain class balance in the test set.

📊 Performance The model achieved high accuracy on the test dataset: | Metric | Value | | :--- | :--- | | Accuracy | 98.12% | | Precision (Class 0) | 1.00 | | Recall (Class 1) | 1.00 |
